opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the data mix was one of the things we spent the most time on, honestly more than people would expect. The starting point is that we wanted one recipe that works across scales, from the 8B up to the 405B, rather than tuning a separate mix for each size. That simplifies the whole pipeline, and it also lets you use the smaller models as a kind of testbed: you run ablations at small scale, look at the scaling behavior, and extrapolate to what's going to happen at the big scale.

The big shifts compared to Llama 2 were, first, way more tokens. We went to around 15 trillion tokens, which is far beyond what Chinchilla-optimal would tell you for an 8B or even a 70B model. But Chinchilla optimizes for training compute, and what we care about is inference. People are going to run these models a lot, so you'd rather overtrain the small ones and get the best possible model at that size. And we saw they just kept improving; they hadn't saturated.

Second, we put a lot of effort into quality filtering and into the composition: more code, more math, more reasoning-heavy data, more multilingual. We used classifiers, and some of them were actually built with Llama 2 itself, to score and filter the web data. Then you decide how much of each domain to include. We did a lot of small-scale experiments where you vary the proportions, fit scaling laws on downstream benchmarks rather than just perplexity, and pick the mix that predicts the best performance at the target scale.

And then at the end of pretraining there's an annealing phase where you upsample very high-quality data, things like math and code, while the learning rate goes down. That gives you a surprisingly big boost, especially on the smaller models. It's also a nice tool for evaluating data: you anneal on a candidate dataset and see whether it moves the needle, which is much cheaper than a full training run.

So the short version: one shared, heavily curated mix, chosen through small-scale experiments and scaling laws, trained well past compute-optimal, with a high-quality annealing stage at the end.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing the mix through small-scale experiments and using high-quality data during final annealing, but does not state that findings during Llama 3’s training led to mix changes within that same training run.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the data mix is one of the places where you can't just reason your way to the answer from first principles, you have to run experiments. And the thing people sometimes miss is that the optimal mix is not the same for every size.

The way we approached it was basically scaling laws, but scaling laws applied to the mix rather than just to compute. We trained a lot of small models on different mixtures, varying the proportions of code, multilingual data, math and reasoning, general web, and so on, and we looked at how downstream benchmarks moved. Not just loss, because loss on a held-out set can be misleading when you change the composition of the data. We cared about what the model could actually do.

Then you take those curves and you extrapolate to the big runs, because at 405B you get one shot. You cannot afford to discover halfway through that you should have had twice as much code. So the small-scale ablations are really a de-risking exercise for the large one.

The number we ended up around for the pretraining mix was roughly half general knowledge, about a quarter math and reasoning, somewhere near seventeen percent code, and the rest multilingual. And the intuition for pushing code and math up, even for a general model, is that they transfer. Code especially improves reasoning across the board, and we saw that in the ablations rather than assuming it.

The other important point is the annealing phase at the end of training. That is where we upsample very high quality data, and that phase is where we could be more aggressive for the smaller models. The small models benefit a lot from that final push on curated data, whereas for the big model you're a bit more careful because it already captured a lot from the raw distribution.

And then one more thing I'd add: the mix interacts with the quantity. Llama 3 was trained on something like fifteen trillion tokens, far beyond what Chinchilla would call optimal for the 8B. We did that on purpose because the goal was not to minimize training compute, it was to produce the best model at inference. When you overtrain like that, the quality and diversity of the mix matter even more, because you're running many epochs over the scarce high-quality sources, and you have to think carefully about deduplication and how many times you want the model to see each piece.

r001.rationale: The response says small-model ablations informed the planned large runs and describes an end-of-training annealing phase, but does not state that findings gathered during Llama 3 training changed its data mix within that same run.

astra-6.text:
We approached it empirically: you choose a mixture, train a model, evaluate it, and adjust. But one of the tricky things is that the best mixture for a small model isn’t necessarily the best mixture for a large one. So you can use smaller models to run experiments cheaply, but you still have to validate that the improvements transfer as you scale up.

And it’s not just about adding more data in a particular domain. If you increase the proportion of code, for example, you want to understand what happens to coding performance, but also to reasoning and general language capabilities. You’re optimizing the whole model, not one benchmark. That’s why the data mix is really an iterative process, alongside data quality and filtering.

sol-6.1.text:
We treated the data mix as something to learn through experiments. You have different sources—web data, code, mathematical content—and you want to understand how changing their proportions affects the capabilities you care about.

The interesting thing is that the best mix isn’t necessarily the same for every model size. A smaller model has less capacity, so the trade-offs between domains can be more pronounced. With a larger model, you have more room to improve several capabilities together. We used smaller-scale experiments to guide those decisions, then checked how well the results transferred as we scaled up.
